qs.q: During a dissection of the axilla, a student notes the intercostobrachial nerve. What is the typical nerve root value of this structure?
qs.e: The intercostobrachial nerve is the lateral cutaneous branch of the second intercostal nerve, giving it a root value of T2. It is clinically relevant during axillary lymph node clearance due to its susceptibility to injury.

qs.q: During a surgical procedure on the axilla, a vessel is identified running along the deltopectoral groove that eventually pierces the clavipectoral fascia to drain into the axillary vein. What is this vessel?
qs.e: The cephalic vein begins at the anatomical snuffbox, ascends the upper limb, travels in the deltopectoral groove, and pierces the clavipectoral fascia to drain into the axillary vein. The basilic vein runs on the medial side of the arm.

qs.q: A 45-year-old man experiences severe chest pain radiating to the medial side of the left arm and the floor of the axilla during angina pectoris. Which nerve mediates this referred pain?
qs.e: Cardiac pain in angina pectoris can be felt in the floor of the axilla via the intercostobrachial nerve distribution. The medial pectoral nerve primarily supplies the pectoral muscles.

qs.q: During a surgical dissection of the axilla, a resident identifies various vascular structures. Which statement about the axillary artery or its major branches is INCORRECT?
o: The second part of the axillary artery lies anterior to the pectoralis minor muscle
The thoracoacromial trunk supplies blood to the deltoid muscle
The lateral thoracic artery supplies blood to the breast
The thoracodorsal artery is the major blood supply to the latissimus dorsi muscle
qs.e: The second part of the axillary artery lies posterior to the pectoralis minor muscle, not anterior to it. The other branches correctly supply their respective regions.

qs.q: A 30-year-old woman has painful red streaks running from a wound on her finger toward her axilla with tender enlarged nodes. Which outcome is most feared if she is not treated urgently?
o: Milroy disease unmasked by acute lymphatic inflammation
Lymphoedema from permanent lymphatic fibrosis after the episode
Bacteraemia and sepsis if bacteria escape the draining lymph nodes into the venous circulation
Chylous ascites from lymphatic hypertension spreading to abdominal lymphatics
qs.e: Lymphangitis (most commonly Group A Streptococcus) tracks bacteria through lymphatics. If not contained within draining nodes, bacteria enter the venous circulation causing bacteraemia and potentially fatal sepsis.

ai.subject: Anatomy
ai.summary: The axilla is a key anatomical space that houses neurovascular bundles, lymphatics, and fat, acting as a conduit between the arm and thorax. Clinically, it is a hub for infection, trauma, and malignancy assessment.

sections.p: The axilla is the triangular space between the upper arm and the thorax, bounded by the clavicle, scapula, and humerus. It serves as a passage for nerves, vessels, and lymphatics, and contains fatty tissue that cushions these structures.
b: Contains fat, nerves, vessels, lymph nodes

sections.p: It lies inferior to the clavicle, medial to the pectoralis major, and lateral to the latissimus dorsi. The axillary fossa is divided into anterior, middle, and posterior compartments by the axillary fascia.

Medially, the pectoralis major; laterally, the latissimus dorsi; posteriorly, the subscapularis and teres major. The axillary vein and artery lie in the middle compartment, while the brachial plexus roots are in the posterior.
The axillary artery, a continuation of the subclavian, gives off the thoracoacromial, lateral thoracic, and subscapular arteries. The axillary vein drains into the subclavian.

t.b: Assesses arterial flow; abnormal flow suggests thrombosis or aneurysm.

sections.p: The brachial plexus passes through the axilla, giving rise to the axillary, radial, median, and ulnar nerves. The thoracodorsal nerve supplies the latissimus dorsi.
b: Axillary nerve injury causes deltoid weakness

t.b: Detects conduction block in radial or axillary nerves.

sections.p: Provides a passage for neurovascular structures and lymphatics, and allows shoulder movement by accommodating the humeral head and scapular motion.
Axillary lymphadenopathy indicates infection or malignancy; trauma can injure the axillary vessels or brachial plexus; infections like candidiasis thrive in moist axillary folds.

t.b: Detects axillary lymphadenopathy secondary to lung cancer.

sections.p: On inspection, look for skin changes, swelling, or erythema. Palpate for lymph nodes and assess shoulder abduction for axillary nerve function.

whenToSeekHelp: Axillary mass that grows rapidly or is hard and fixed
Severe pain with swelling suggesting abscess or vascular injury
Sudden loss of shoulder abduction indicating brachial plexus injury

faq.a: Moist, warm skin folds with poor hygiene, especially in diabetics or immunocompromised patients.

faq.q: How to differentiate axillary lymphadenitis from lymphoma?
faq.a: Reactive nodes are usually tender and fluctuate; lymphoma nodes are often firm, non‑tender, and may be fixed.

faq.q: Why is the axillary vein important in central line placement?
faq.a: It is a common site for central venous access; injury can lead to massive bleeding or air embolism.
